title: Don’t Blame Ukraine for High Gas Prices
gist: Keith Johnson argues the true driver of ~$105 crude, $4.29 gasoline and record $6 diesel is the six-month-old U.S.-Israel war on Iran, not Ukraine's refinery strikes: independent tanker trackers put Hormuz flows at 8-9 mb/d versus 20 mb/d pre-war, the Saudi East-West bypass pipeline is now itself under Houthi attack, and global refinery throughput is 5 mb/d below last year.

themes.theme: The refining bottleneck, not crude supply

insights.claim: Global refinery throughput remains 5 million barrels a day below last year's average even with U.S. refineries running flat out, because Russian, Middle Eastern and some Chinese refiners are offline — making refining, not crude or chokepoints, the binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Crack spreads, not flat crude price, are where the scarcity is priced — favors refiners with intact capacity and argues product spreads stay elevated longer than crude.
insights.quote: The International Energy Agency says global refinery throughput remains 5 million barrels a day below last year’s average, and that is with U.S. refineries running flat out.

insights.claim: U.S. diesel reached $6 a gallon for the first time ever and gasoline spiked to $4.29 a gallon, up a dollar year-over-year, with Brent-equivalent benchmark crude around $105 after breaking $100.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Record diesel is the more economically damaging print — it feeds directly into freight, agriculture and industrial costs, sustaining goods inflation.
insights.quote: U.S. average gasoline prices spiked to $4.29 a gallon (up a dollar from a year ago), while the much more important price of diesel reached $6 a gallon for the first time ever.

insights.claim: Ukrainian drone strikes have destroyed an estimated 12-15 percent of total Russian refinery throughput but cannot take capacity offline permanently — drones are light, repairs are easy, and many strikes halt production for only a day or so.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Russian refinery outages are recurring but mean-reverting; don't extrapolate individual strike headlines into persistent supply loss.
insights.quote: Our estimate is that the destroyed capacity is 12-15 percent of total Russian refinery throughput
insights.locator: But to go back to the first point

insights.claim: Russia is now importing gasoline as its refined product exports decline and its domestic energy distribution system comes under sustained stress.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: A net-exporter turned importer of gasoline is a meaningful shift in global product balances and a signal of genuine domestic strain in Russia.
insights.locator: The latest numbers on Russian fossil fuel exports

insights.claim: Elevated diesel costs hit U.S. farmers at harvest season on top of already higher fertilizer and farm equipment prices, compounding agricultural cost inflation.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Farm margin compression argues for agricultural input cost pass-through and potential political pressure for farm support ahead of midterms.
insights.locator: That is a problem for everyone

themes.theme: Hormuz is far more closed than officials admit

insights.claim: Independent tanker trackers counting individual ships, loadings, ship-to-ship transfers and final port calls put Strait of Hormuz flows at roughly 8-9 million barrels a day on average, versus 20 million b/d before the war — contradicting U.S. official claims the strait is open.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: A ~11 mb/d gap between official narrative and ship-count data is the single most important mispriced input in oil markets right now — trust tanker trackers over official statements.
insights.quote: Independent tanker trackers, which count individual ships, their loadings, ship-to-ship transfers, and those ships’ final port calls, put the number at closer to 8-9 million barrels a day, on average.
insights.locator: There is a very entertaining debate

insights.claim: Iranian forces periodically blow up tankers that attempt to transit Hormuz, suppressing the recovery in flows — a single tanker left the Persian Gulf on the Thursday before publication.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Transit risk is being enforced kinetically, so war-risk insurance and charter rates for Gulf routes will stay punitive regardless of political statements.
insights.quote: A single tanker left the Persian Gulf on Thursday.
insights.locator: That low number and the slow pace of recovery

insights.claim: The U.S. military has destroyed 12 of roughly 60 tankers in the Iranian fleet in response to Iranian attacks on U.S. ships and U.S.-escorted tankers.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Twenty percent fleet attrition on a shadow-fleet operator sets a precedent for kinetic enforcement against sanctioned shipping — a risk repricing for the entire dark fleet.
insights.locator: All of this comes at a time of escalation

insights.claim: The tanker destruction matters little to Tehran because the U.S. naval blockade means Iran is barely exporting crude or refined products at all, and the Iranian economy has been built since 1979 to withstand pain.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Economic pressure is unlikely to force Iranian capitulation on a market-relevant timeline — plan for a prolonged supply disruption rather than a quick resolution.
insights.locator: That is less of a problem for Tehran

themes.theme: The bypass is being bypassed: Red Sea and East-West pipeline

insights.claim: The Saudi-led overland workaround to Hormuz — principally the East-West pipeline from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea — was running at full blast shipping about 5 million barrels a day, but is now reportedly under direct Houthi attack.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: If the last 5 mb/d workaround is degraded, the effective Gulf export ceiling collapses further — the single most important escalation to watch for oil price tails.
insights.quote: But they, too, are now under threat.

insights.claim: The Houthis have seized the Hanish Islands and Zuqar and may soon take Mayun (Perim Island), the key island in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, giving them and Iran far greater scope to influence shipping movements, insurance premiums and energy transport costs.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Physical control of Bab el-Mandeb islands converts harassment into durable leverage over Suez routing — a structural upward shift in Red Sea insurance and tanker rates.
insights.quote: Together, these positions would give the Houthis—and by extension, Iran—far greater scope to influence shipping movements, insurance premiums, and the cost of transporting energy and other commodities.
insights.locator: The Houthis, an Iran-backed rebel group in Yemen

insights.claim: Continued Houthi attacks on tankers staging near Yanbu, the Saudi Red Sea port, could discourage use of the only real workaround to the Hormuz blockage.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Both Gulf export routes are now contested simultaneously — the probability-weighted supply risk is higher than either chokepoint assessed alone.
insights.locator: But the Houthis have apparently escalated

themes.theme: Political blame-shifting ahead of the midterms

insights.claim: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has publicly blamed Ukraine's drone and missile strikes on Russian refineries for record U.S. pump prices — a claim the article's evidence contradicts.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Official U.S. energy attribution is politically motivated; use it as a sentiment indicator on midterm pressure rather than as analysis.
insights.locator: In recent interviews, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright

insights.claim: Trump offered voters $5,000 in cash to vote Republican in the November midterms — an amount the author benchmarks at 830 gallons of diesel — and said the Iran war will continue through the midterms.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: An explicit political commitment to continue the war through November removes the near-term de-escalation scenario from the oil price path.
insights.quote: Trump this week said the Iran war will continue through the midterms, but it is not clear he is running the clock.
insights.locator: That is less of a problem for Tehran

insights.claim: Gasoline prices are the most significant issue ahead of U.S. elections, and because Trump cannot be blamed politically, Zelensky is blamed instead.
insights.speaker: Keith Johnson
insights.so_what: Political need for a scapegoat raises the risk of policy actions against Ukraine's strike campaign — a watch item for Russian refining recovery and product supply.
insights.quote: Gasoline prices in the United States are the most significant issue ahead of elections, but nobody can blame Trump. So they blame [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelensky.
